An application ping does more, since it also proves the process is working, not only the kernel.

Q · Trade-off — TCP keepalive or an application heartbeat? Keepalive reaps dead sockets and holds middlebox state, with no protocol change. Use a heartbeat when you need to know the service is alive, because a deadlocked process still answers keepalives from its kernel. Watch what counts as activity: AWS's ALB docs say HTTP/2 PING frames don't reset its idle timeout.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Keepalive floor ≥ 2 hours, off by default RFC rule for any implementation spec: RFC 9293 §3.8.4
macOS detection 7,800 s 7,200 + 8 × 75, keepcnt 8 derived, sysctl 1 Nov 2026
Linux with unacked data 924.6 s hypothetical tcp_retries2 = 15 default (as of Nov 2026): Linux ip-sysctl

Pitfalls

  • "Keepalive is on, so dead connections get cleaned up"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the word appears in configs, and HTTP keep-alive is on by default.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: SO_KEEPALIVE starts at 0, as the capture shows, and even when enabled the first probe waits two hours.
    ↳ Think instead: no configuration means no keepalive. Enable it per socket, with your own timers.
  • Not the same: TCP keepalive vs HTTP keep-alive
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: they share a name, and both concern connections staying open.
    ↳ Difference: TCP keepalive sends probes on an idle socket. HTTP keep-alive reuses a connection for more requests and sends nothing extra.
    ↳ Think instead: probe vs reuse. A connection can use either, both or neither.
  • "ESTABLISHED means the peer is reachable"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: that's what netstat appears to say.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's this kernel's record. The peer may have rebooted, and a NAT entry may be gone; nothing tells you until you send.
    ↳ Think instead: a local belief. Only a recent ACK says anything about the peer.
  • Don't set a pool's idle limit equal to the LB's.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: matching numbers looks tidy, and it passes every test.
    ↳ What goes wrong: equal timers race, giving rare resets that can't be reproduced and that consume days.
    ↳ Do instead: leave a clear margin, and just retire pooled connections early: a max-age is simpler than tuning keepalive.
  • Shelf life: the RFC rule is durable. Vendor idle limits change: re-check the Landscape on schedule.

Connections

Path:teardownkeepalives and half-open connectionsconnection pooling
  • Owned elsewhere: connection pooling owns the idle-timeout inequality and pool sizing.
  • Contrasts with teardown: an orderly close that leaves a signal.
  • Composes with NAT: its timers are why probes exist on long-lived flows.
  • Used by WebSocket in production: heartbeats against LB idle limits.

References

📜 RFC 6335 §6: Port Number Ranges · 📜 RFC 6056: Port Randomization · Linux IP sysctls · Cloudflare: running out of ephemeral ports · Kegel: The C10K problem

TL;DR

A connection is named by four values: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. A server on one port varies none of its own and still holds any number of them, because the client supplies the variety, so the scarce resource sits on the client side. Servers run out of descriptors and memory. Clients calling one upstream run out of source ports, and TIME_WAIT turns that count into a rate.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:connect()kernel picks a free source port4-tuple must be uniqueconnection usedclient closes firstport held by TIME_WAITrange emptyEADDRNOTAVAIL

Recall

Prompt Answer
What identifies a connection? Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port.
Default ephemeral range? Linux 32768–60999, 28,232 ports. macOS 49152–65535, 16,384 ports.
Server out of descriptors vs client out of ports? EMFILE vs EADDRNOTAVAIL.

The idea

A gateway opens a new connection to one backend per request, and at a few hundred requests a second it fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL. CPU is idle, and nobody has seen that error before. "A server can't pass 65,535 connections" is the wrong story: the server here is fine, and it's the gateway that can't find a source port.

The 4-tuple explains both. To one destination, only the source port varies, so that range is the budget, and TIME_WAIT makes each used port unavailable for a while. Reuse removes the problem by no longer spending ports at all.

The trade: a short-lived connection costs a port for the whole TIME_WAIT, so connection churn hits a rate ceiling long before any hardware limit.

How it works

The server varies nothing and the client supplies the difference, so the budget lands on the client.

The owner's arithmetic for the ceiling; every other note links here:

sustained new connections = ports ÷ TIME_WAIT seconds     ← active closer, one destination
Linux default = 28,232 ÷ 60 ≈ 470/s                       ← 32768–60999
macOS default = 16,384 ÷ 30 ≈ 546/s                       ← 49152–65535, 2 × 15 s MSL
Rule What actually happens
Listen port vs connection Accepted sockets share the listener's port; each is told apart by the peer. Ports are per protocol, so TCP 443 and UDP 443 are separate.
Budget per what? Linux reuses a source port across destinations in a plain connect(), so the budget is per destination. macOS failed for a new destination too (below), so don't assume this elsewhere.
Random ports RFC 6056 randomises the source port to resist off-path attacks, and suggests using 1024–65535. Defaults are narrower.
tcp_tw_reuse Linux default 2: loopback only. Set to 1 it reuses TIME_WAIT tuples for outbound connections when timestamps allow.
The middle A NAT or proxy is a client too, and funnels many sources into one IP: AWS quotes 55,000 per destination for a NAT gateway IP (NAT).

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the port rules are decades old, and C10K-scale servers are ordinary. The limits moved from select() to memory.
  • Changed in Linux: bind() before connect() can burn the port for every destination; IP_BIND_ADDRESS_NO_PORT (Linux 4.2) defers the choice to connect().
  • What's next: nothing protocol-level. What won't change: four values, and the arithmetic above.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15, macOS 27.0.1). Each run is a short loop; the second holds about 16,000 ports for 30 s, so don't run it on a busy machine.

# 256-descriptor limit, connect and accept in a loop, keep everything open
held 252 sockets: OSError(24, 'Too many open files')     # EMFILE; the accepted side all on port 51672
# connect, accept, client closes first, in a loop against one port
after 16144 connections in 0.6 s: OSError(49, "Can't assign requested address")   # EADDRNOTAVAIL
new destination port → OSError(49, ...)                  # the same error against a different port

The second line is the ceiling for real: 16,144 of 16,384 ports gone in 0.6 s. The third contradicts the usual story: the budget wasn't per destination on macOS. The per-destination claim for Linux is Cloudflare's.

Measure it

  • See it: netstat -an -p tcp | grep -c TIME_WAIT on macOS, ss -s on Linux; sysctl net.inet.ip.portrange.first or net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range shows the range; ulimit -n shows descriptors.
  • In production: per host, new connections per second against the ceiling, TIME_WAIT count, open descriptors against the limit, and EADDRNOTAVAIL or EMFILE in client logs. Socket state owns the reading.
  • Bounded by: port exhaustion → a connection pool, more destination IPs, a wider range last; descriptor exhaustion → a raised limit plus a connection cap, so you shed load before memory runs out.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A connection is a four-tuple, so one server port can hold millions: clients supply the variation. The limit is on the client: to one upstream only the source port varies, 28,232 of them on default Linux. With TIME_WAIT holding each for 60 seconds, that's about 470 new connections a second. So pool. Servers hit descriptors and memory instead, and the first symptom is EMFILE.

Q · Mechanism — "A server can only hold 65,535 connections." What's wrong with that? It confuses a listening port with a connection's identity. The server listens on 443, and every accepted socket shares that local port, as the capture shows. What tells them apart is the peer's address and port. So the 65,535 limit is on services per address. A server's ceiling is one descriptor per connection, against ulimit -n (DefaultLimitNOFILE under systemd is 1024:524288), plus kernel memory for data in flight. Ports bind only where one side is fixed, which is the client.

Q · Trade-off — Your gateway hits EADDRNOTAVAIL against one backend. What do you change? Reuse first: at 470 requests a second and 20 ms, about ten are in flight, so a small pool replaces all that churn (connection pooling owns sizing). Second, add backend IPs, which multiplies the budget on Linux. Third, tcp_tw_reuse=1. Widening the range to 10240–65535 only doubles it.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
IANA dynamic range 49152–65535 macOS default matches spec: RFC 6335 §6
Linux ephemeral range 32768–60999, 28,232 ports ip_local_port_range default (as of Nov 2026): Linux ip-sysctl
macOS exhaustion 16,144 connects in 0.6 s single run, loopback measured 1 Nov 2026, macOS 27.0.1
Linux descriptors 1024:524288 soft:hard under systemd default (as of Nov 2026): systemd-system.conf(5)

Pitfalls

  • "One port means 65,535 connections at most"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a 16-bit port number sounds like the obvious ceiling.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: that counts ports, while connections count 4-tuples. Every accepted socket in the capture shares one local port.
    ↳ Think instead: servers run out of descriptors and memory. The port ceiling is a client's, facing one upstream.
  • Not the same: EMFILE vs EADDRNOTAVAIL
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both arrive as "can't connect" under load, and both are unfamiliar.
    ↳ Difference: EMFILE means this process is out of descriptors. EADDRNOTAVAIL means no source port is free for that tuple.
    ↳ Think instead: descriptors are concurrency, ports are rate. Hold connections and you hit the first; churn them and you hit the second.
  • Don't start with sysctls.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: widening the range is one line and it works today.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you buy twice the rate on a limit that a pool removes, and you hide the churn that will hit a NAT next.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler fix: one shared client with keep-alive.
  • Don't size memory from the buffer limit alone, or assume idle is free.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: multiplying a buffer limit by connections looks like capacity planning.
    ↳ What goes wrong: those limits are ceilings, so the sum overstates idle sockets and understates a slow-client pile-up, when queues really fill.
    ↳ Do instead: measure per-connection memory under your real traffic, including slow readers.
  • Shelf life: the arithmetic is durable. OS defaults and each kernel's port-reuse rules are what to re-check.

Connections

Path:teardownsockets and portskeepalives
  • Builds on teardown: TIME_WAIT turns a port count into a rate.
  • Bounded by connection pooling: the control that removes the churn.
  • Composes with NAT: the same arithmetic on a shared gateway.
  • Measured by socket state: reading counts on a live host.

notes.title: When UDP Is Right — and What You Then Owe
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 8085: UDP Usage Guidelines (BCP 145) · 📜 RFC 768: User Datagram Protocol · 📜 RFC 1035 §4.2: DNS transport · HPBN: Building Blocks of UDP

TL;DR

UDP is right when a resend would arrive too late to matter, or when the exchange is so short that a handshake would dominate it. Everything TCP gave you is then yours to rebuild or to do without, and pacing is the one you can't skip. If you find yourself adding ACKs and retransmission, stop: that's QUIC, already written.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:still useful after 1 RTT?UDPsize under the path MTUpace itheartbeat for NATcount your own lossTCP fallback for clients

Recall

Prompt Answer
The one-line test? Is the data worthless by the time a resend could arrive?
Safe payload without path knowledge? 1,232 bytes: 1,280 − 40 − 8, the IPv6 minimum path.
The duty you can't skip? Congestion control, or a low rate with a circuit breaker.

The idea

A 20 ms audio frame that arrives 200 ms late isn't late audio, it's noise. TCP's one tool is retransmission, so it stalls the stream to deliver something the listener no longer needs. On UDP the frame is simply missing, the jitter buffer conceals it, and the next frame plays on time.

That's the real test. It then creates debts TCP used to pay: nobody paces you, sizes your packets, keeps NAT entries alive or reports loss.

The trade: you gain control over what happens on loss, and you pay by owning pacing, sizing, reachability and visibility.

How it works

Each legitimate use keeps a different subset of what TCP offered, so the debts differ too. "Which one?" is the chapter map's decision tree; this table is what each answer owes.

Use Why UDP What it adds back When UDP fails
DNS a handshake would double a tiny lookup client retry, truncation bit same query over TCP (RFC 9210: both are mandatory)
Voice and video (RTP) late audio is worthless jitter buffer, concealment, FEC TURN over TCP, at a quality cost
QUIC transport in userspace, per-stream delivery everything, in the library HTTP/2 over TCP via Alt-Svc
Metrics never block the app nothing, loss is accepted batched HTTP where loss matters
Discovery (mDNS) multicast, which TCP can't do periodic re-announcement a unicast registry

What you owe, from RFC 8085:

Rule What actually happens
Pacing §3.1: control your rate across all flows to a destination. Bulk senders use TCP-like control; low-volume ones send at most about one datagram per RTT; otherwise add a circuit breaker.
Size §3.2: don't exceed the path MTU; if unknown, assume 576 bytes on IPv4 and 1,280 on IPv6.
Keepalive §3.5: no more often than every 15 s. RFC 4787 asks NATs for 2 minutes or more, and RFC 8085 notes many use less.
The middle No flags, so firewalls run timers or block. An NLB tracks a UDP flow for 120 s, then treats the next packet as a new flow, possibly to a new target. 
max payload = MTU − IP header − UDP header     ← fragmenting is the thing to avoid
Ethernet    = 1500 − 20 − 8  = 1,472 bytes     ← IPv4, no tunnel
safe        = 1280 − 40 − 8  = 1,232 bytes     ← DNS Flag Day 2020's default
P(lost)     = 1 − (1 − p)^n                    ← n fragments: lose one, lose the datagram

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): RFC 768 stands from 1980, and QUIC made UDP a substrate.
  • Changed in RFC 8085 (Mar 2017): obsoleted RFC 5405 and added multicast, anycast and tunnels.
  • What's next: datagram extensions on QUIC for media. What won't change: a datagram doesn't care whether it arrived.

On the wire

Captured 1 Nov 2026 on 127.0.0.1 (Python 3.15, macOS 27.0.1): 2,000 datagrams of 1,200 bytes sent at a receiver with a 64 KB buffer that isn't reading yet.

r.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_RCVBUF, 65536)   # small on purpose
for i in range(2000): s.sendto(b"x" * 1200, r.getsockname())
# → sender: 2000 of 2000 sendto() calls succeeded
# → receiver: got 54
# netstat -s -p udp, "dropped due to full socket buffers": 0 → 1946

No error reached either application, and the kernel's counter is the only evidence. A separate test sent 9,216 bytes and failed at 9,217 with EMSGSIZE, macOS's net.inet.udp.maxdgram cap.

Measure it

  • See it: netstat -s -p udp on macOS, nstat -az UdpRcvbufErrors UdpInErrors on Linux; compare before and after a burst.
  • In production: per receiver, buffer drops; per flow, your own sequence gaps and arrival jitter; per client cohort, the share on the TCP fallback. A fallback share creeping up means you've lost the benefit quietly.
  • Bounded by: an unpaced flood → rate limits and a circuit breaker (RFC 8085 §3.1.10); silent loss → per-flow sequence numbers and drop alerts; a blocked path → a monitored TCP fallback.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: UDP fits when a resend would arrive too late to matter, such as live audio or game state, or when a handshake would dominate a tiny exchange, such as DNS. Then you own what TCP did: sizing under the path MTU, keepalives for NAT, loss counters, a fallback, and above all congestion control. If you need reliability and ordering too, use QUIC rather than rebuild it.

Q · Mechanism — Why does DNS use both transports? Queries are small, so UDP avoids a handshake. If a reply won't fit, the server sets the truncation bit and the client asks again over TCP. RFC 1035 §4.2 set 512 bytes, EDNS raised it, and DNS Flag Day 2020 settled on 1,232. RFC 9210 makes TCP mandatory, so filtering it is an outage in waiting (DNS resolution owns the rest).

Q · Trade-off — Your UDP protocol now needs ordering and acknowledgement. What do you do? Stop and use QUIC. Sequence numbers lead to ACKs, retransmission and a window, and you arrive at a worse TCP. The UDP protocols that last never added reliability: RTP conceals loss, DNS retries the whole query. If only one message type needs delivery, carry it over a reliable channel beside the datagrams.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Unknown-path size 576 IPv4, 1,280 IPv6 default effective send MTU spec: RFC 8085 §3.2
EDNS buffer default 1,232 bytes 1,280 − 48 default (as of Nov 2026): DNS Flag Day 2020
NAT mapping floor ≥ 2 min, 5 min advised port-specific exceptions below 1024 spec: RFC 4787 REQ-5

Pitfalls

  • "UDP is the choice when you need speed"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no handshake and a small header sound fast.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the header saving is trivial at real payloads, and bulk data on UDP needs pacing and recovery, which is TCP's job.
    ↳ Think instead: the test is expiry, not speed: does the data lose its value before a resend?
  • Not the same: QUIC vs "UDP with my own reliability"
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are reliable transports running over UDP.
    ↳ Difference: QUIC is standardised (RFC 9000, 9002), tested at scale and congestion controlled. Yours is a private protocol with none of that.
    ↳ Think instead: adding retransmission means choosing QUIC, not writing it.
  • Don't pick UDP when batched HTTP would do.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the word "telemetry" points at UDP.
    ↳ What goes wrong: at modest rates you give up retries, TLS, auth and proxies, and build loss counters to recover visibility.
    ↳ Do instead: batch into HTTP POSTs, and move only when volume or blocking proves the need.
  • Don't ship client-facing UDP without a watched fallback.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it works on your network, and the fallback code never fires in tests.
    ↳ What goes wrong: blocked users fail or fall back silently, and you've paid for a benefit they never got.
    ↳ Do instead: build the TCP path, and chart the share of traffic using it.
  • Shelf life: RFC 768 and the expiry test are durable. Advice on middlebox blocking and QUIC reach is what to re-check.

Connections

Path:TCP vs UDPwhen UDP is rightQUIC
  • Builds on congestion control: the duty you inherit.
  • Owned elsewhere: MTU and PMTUD owns fragmentation and path discovery.
  • Used by ICE, STUN and TURN: NAT traversal and the fallback path.
  • Composes with NAT: why long UDP flows need heartbeats.
  • Drilled in WebRTC or WebSocket: the audio-transport version.
